crm_note.headline: Sofia Marchetti debriefed after second round at Fernhallow Capital; office policy is her main concern
crm_note.how_it_went: Sofia described the day as intense but said she enjoyed it, which she had not expected. She said she was much stronger on the portfolio case than on the coding, where she missed a ticker change until Nadia hinted. On Graham Lowe's market intuition question she felt she was OK but not sharp.

rounds.format: Coding with Nadia. The format was changed in the week before the call: pandas documentation was open in a browser and allowed, but nothing else (no search, no AI tools).
asked: Messy prices data with delisted names (survivorship)
An unadjusted ten-for-one split, giving a fake crash in the return series
A ticker that changed halfway through after a company rename
Build a twelve-one momentum signal, rank it and look at the long-short (momentum, not reversal)
rounds.candidate_view: Sofia flagged survivorship straight away and could see Nadia was happy. She caught the split but completely missed the ticker change until Nadia hinted: "look at the names that start and stop on the same day". She said she was much stronger on the case than on the coding.

rounds.format: Graham Lowe joined for the first fifteen minutes
asked: Expected value of the maximum of two independent uniforms on zero to one (Sofia answered two thirds)
Market intuition: factor crowding this year and the momentum unwind in the spring
rounds.candidate_view: She had not prepped the market intuition question at all. She talked about crowding and deleveraging and thought it was OK but not sharp. Graham was totally flat and gave nothing away; she did not panic because she had been told to expect that.

rounds.format: Case with Nadia and Pieter (not the bad backtest case)
asked: How to turn a signal with an IC of about 0.03 into a portfolio: sizing, turnover, how costs eat it, and capacity
rounds.candidate_view: She said she was much stronger on this than on the coding, as she does this every day at Ketterby.

rounds.format: Marcus came in at the end for about ten minutes, standing
asked: What would make her kill a signal
rounds.candidate_view: She answered a pre-agreed drawdown and decay rule, set before the signal goes live. Marcus said "that's the right order" and left.

compensation.notes: Compensation did not come up in the interview.

crm_note.notice_and_non_compete: Twelve weeks' notice, no non-compete. Sofia told Nadia this in the interview and Nadia said "that's nice to hear for once".
competing_processes: Asset manager in Paris: second round in the week starting 2026-11-30
risks: Office policy: Nadia said the team is in the office five days a week, and Hannah had understood four. Sofia said this might be a problem because her partner is in Milan half the month, and called it her real worry. She said Fernhallow is her first choice if the office question works.
Paris asset manager process is moving, with a second round in the week starting 2026-11-30.

next_actions.action: Call Ingrid for feedback on the second round
Ask Ingrid about the office attendance policy (five days versus four)
Talk the office question through properly with Sofia
Start picking a project for the research presentation with Marcus (the final stage)

process.format: Video call of about forty-five minutes. About ten minutes on your CV, then probability questions typed into a shared document. No coding.
process.what_they_look_for: Careful reasoning and checking your own answers on probability. On the CV, how you validated your work: crash periods, true out-of-sample testing and who chose the holdout. Graham gives no reaction during the call.

process.format: Held at the office, in two parts of about an hour each. First hour: a short probability warm-up, then live Python on a provided laptop using messy daily price and volume data. Since the week before 24 Nov, the pandas documentation is open in a browser, but there is no search and no AI tools. Before that change there was no internet at all. Second hour: a stats or research case. At least once, Graham Lowe joined the first fifteen minutes of the second hour for a probability question and a market intuition question. Marcus Elling has also come in at the end for about ten minutes to ask one question.
process.who: Nadia Osei (researcher, equities) for the coding. Nadia and Pieter (researcher, surname not caught) for the case. Graham Lowe and Marcus Elling (PM) have also joined briefly.
process.what_they_look_for: Spotting data problems before computing anything (delisted names and survivorship bias, unadjusted splits, ticker changes, bad prints). Nadia said she cares about the logic rather than exact syntax. In the case, rigour on backtest flaws, transaction costs and turning a signal into a portfolio.

process.format: About three hours in total. A research presentation on a past project you can discuss without breaking confidentiality: thirty minutes to present, then questions for the rest of the hour. Then thirty minutes with the head of research. A further fifteen-minute one-to-one with the PM followed.
process.who: Marcus Elling (PM), researchers Nadia and Felix, and Ingrid Saarinen (head of research)
process.what_they_look_for: Whether a signal survives factor neutralisation, why it works economically and who is on the other side of the trade, and clear rules for when to switch a signal off. Ingrid covered culture, how you like to work and how you deal with being wrong.

examples: Expected number of rolls of a fair die until you see a six
Expected number of coin flips until you get two heads in a row, then the heads-then-tails version
Three random points on a circle: probability the triangle contains the centre
A stick broken at two random points: chance the three pieces make a triangle
Expected value of the maximum of two independent uniforms on zero to one

question_themes.theme: Live Python on messy equity data
examples: Build a simple reversal signal and say what the performance looks like
Build twelve-one momentum, rank it and look at the long-short
A backtest with a Sharpe of about 2.1: what's wrong with this?
How many variants do you think were tried to get this one?
How would you model market impact for small caps, and at what participation rate?

question_themes.theme: Turning a signal into a portfolio
examples: A signal with an IC of about 0.03: how would you turn it into a portfolio, covering sizing, turnover, how costs eat it, and capacity (how much money before it stops working)?

question_themes.theme: When to switch a signal off
examples: What would make you kill this signal?
How long would you wait: are you going to sit through six months of drawdown?
What do you think about the factor crowding this year and the momentum unwind in the spring?
How do you handle crash periods such as 2009 in momentum work?
Did you test out of sample properly or tune on the whole history?
Who chose the holdout?
Is this just value in disguise: have you neutralised against the standard factors?
Why does it work economically, and who is on the other side of the trade?
How do you like to work?
How do you deal with being wrong?

went_well: On the two-heads-in-a-row question, giving four, then correcting to six and walking through the states, drew "good, you checked it" from Graham.
In the coding task, asking why some series end (delisted or acquired) before computing anything, and naming survivorship bias, drew a smile from Nadia.
In the coding task, flagging survivorship straight away on the delisted names visibly pleased Nadia.
Saying "I'd normally check the docs here" and writing the intended logic in pseudo-pandas drew Nadia's comment that this was fine and that she cares about the logic.
When asked "is this just value in disguise", showing a backup slide with the factor-neutral version (the effect drops but remains) drew "OK, good" from Marcus.
On when to kill a signal, cutting the size rather than killing it outright, and setting the rule before going live, drew a lot of nodding from Felix.
On what would make you kill a signal, a pre-agreed drawdown and decay rule set before it goes live drew "that's the right order" from Marcus.
tripped_people_up: In the backtest case, Nadia and Pieter pushed hard on costs, including market impact for small caps and participation rate, and the answer given was hand-wavy.
A ticker change partway through the data, caused by a company renaming, was missed until Nadia hinted: "look at the names that start and stop on the same day".
On out-of-sample testing, a holdout from 2019 onwards drew Graham's follow-up of who chose the holdout, and it had been self-chosen.
advice: Before computing any signal, check the data for series that stop (delisted or acquired), unadjusted splits that create fake crashes, ticker changes and bad prints, and say what you find out loud.
You can use the pandas documentation but nothing else. If you cannot recall syntax, say so and write out the logic clearly.
Practise quick probability puzzles (stopping times, geometric probability, order statistics) for the warm-up. If Graham appears, expect no reaction from him either way.
Prepare a concrete view on transaction costs: how you would model market impact for small caps and what participation rate you would assume.

Be ready for either case: critiquing a too-good backtest (look-ahead, costs and turnover, multiple testing and deflating the Sharpe) or turning a low-IC signal into a portfolio (sizing, turnover, costs, capacity).
Have a clear answer on when you would switch a signal off, with the rule agreed before it goes live and a view on cutting size versus killing it.
Have a view on factor crowding this year and the spring momentum unwind, in case a market intuition question comes up.
For the final, pick a project you can present without breaking confidentiality, prepare a factor-neutral backup, and be able to explain who is on the other side of the trade.
logistics: The coding part of the second round changed in the week before 24 Nov: the pandas documentation is now open in a browser, with no search and no AI tools. You use a laptop they provide.
The firm asks about notice period and non-compete in every round: Graham in the first, Nadia in the second, and Ingrid in the final.
Ingrid stated that it is firm policy not to buy out garden leave.
Your record shows 8 weeks' notice and a 3-month non-compete, so have these ready.
Nadia said the team is in the office five days a week.
At the final, Marcus asked for references before any offer.
